topicsShown.title: Lead a short team meeting
topicsShown.goal: Open a meeting, invite ideas and confirm who will do each task.
topicsShown.why: You want to run meetings, so you will practise guiding a short team discussion.

topicsShown.title: Agree on a supplier deadline
topicsShown.goal: Explain when you need an order, discuss options and agree on a delivery plan.
topicsShown.why: You want to negotiate deadlines with suppliers and reach a clear agreement.

topicsShown.title: Chat with a visiting US director
topicsShown.goal: Start a friendly conversation and keep it going with a follow-up question.
topicsShown.why: You want to feel prepared for small talk with a US director.

topicsShown.title: Present a quality problem
topicsShown.goal: Explain what went wrong, how you found it and what happened next.
topicsShown.why: You want to present quality problems clearly, with events in a useful order.

topicsShown.title: Check what a meeting decision means
topicsShown.goal: Ask for a clearer explanation and confirm a task and its deadline.
topicsShown.why: Checking meaning helps you leave meetings with a clear plan.

topicsShown.title: Ask for useful photos of a fault
topicsShown.goal: Request clear photos, explain what they should show and confirm when they will arrive.
topicsShown.why: Useful details help you prepare a clear presentation about a quality problem.

topicsShown.title: Ask for help with a new work tool
topicsShown.goal: Explain what you need to do and agree on a short training session with a colleague.
topicsShown.why: This helps you explain work needs, give reasons and make a practical plan in English.

topicsShown.title: Tell a colleague how a project went
topicsShown.goal: Explain the main steps of a finished project, what helped, and what you would do differently.
topicsShown.why: This builds the clear explanations and connected workplace talk you want for meetings.

topicsShown.title: Disagree politely and decide next steps
topicsShown.goal: Explain why a deadline cannot work, compare solutions and agree on a realistic next step.
topicsShown.why: You want to explain your solution clearly and reach a decision without a long argument.

criteria.evidence: No placement tasks or verdict occur in this journey. Steps #1 and #7 display “B1 · Getting by”; this does not establish placement accuracy.
No placement explanation is presented in this journey. Step #1 starts at “Choose your topics”.
This journey contains topic planning, with no moments or coaching notes. Step #5 supplies “we was discussing about supplier delay” as topic input.
No corrections are shown. Steps #2–#6 collect preferences, propose topics, support swaps and additions, and accept the plan.

Five of the initial six topics fit his workplace-meeting needs. Step #3 includes “Lead a short team meeting”, “Agree on a supplier deadline”, “Chat with a visiting US director” and “Present a quality problem”; facts.topicsShown also includes “Check what a meeting decision means”.
He never asks why a correction is wrong in steps #1–#7; step #5 asks for practice “disagreeing politely with stakeholder”.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears. All nine proposed topics are safe for this adult profile. There are no facts.conversation turns or moments to score.

findings.title: The agreed plan fits his meeting responsibilities
findings.expected: Most topics should be conversations Martin would choose, with reasons connected to his goals.
findings.got: Seven of nine distinct proposals fit, and all seven agreed topics fit. The two rejected proposals concern fault photos and training on a work tool.
findings.evidence: Step #3 explains, “You want to negotiate deadlines with suppliers and reach a clear agreement.” Step #6: “Good, these are useful for my work”. facts.planAgreed records seven relevant topics. Step #7 confirms “Next from your plan: Lead a short team meeting”.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve explicit links between workplace goals and proposals, with at least four relevant topics in the initial six.

findings.title: An explicit stakeholder goal required repeated steering
findings.expected: Include polite stakeholder disagreement from his initial request, or offer it promptly when replacing an unwanted topic.
findings.got: The initial set omitted that goal. Two swaps produced other workplace topics, and Martin had to repeat the request through Add.
findings.evidence: Step #2 requests “how to disagree politely when stakeholder don't agree with my solution”. Step #3 rejects photos; step #4 says, “Asking for help with a tool is too basic for me”. Step #5 repeats, “I want practise disagreeing politely with stakeholder”. facts.topicsShown records both rejected proposals.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Cover each distinct explicitly requested situation before filling slots with adjacent work activities.

findings.title: The custom topic preserves his practical intent
findings.expected: An added topic should retain the stakeholder conflict, unrealistic deadline and decision-making objective.
findings.got: The added topic retains those elements and is saved in the agreed plan.
findings.evidence: Step #5 asks about an “impossible deadline” and making “a decision without long argument”. facts.topicsShown gives the added goal as “Explain why a deadline cannot work, compare solutions and agree on a realistic next step.” Step #6 agrees; facts.planAgreed includes “Disagree politely and decide next steps”.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Keep custom-topic meaning intact through generation and agreement.

judge.voice: Look, the meeting topics are useful: supplier deadlines, quality problems, talking with the US director. I would use this plan again. But I asked for stakeholder disagreement at the start, and I still had to reject two suggestions and type it again. Once I added it, the result kept what I meant. That matters. I still think B1 is too low; this journey gave me no reason to change my mind, and I have not seen corrections to judge. There is no timing evidence here, so I cannot claim it saves my weekly lesson or is worth particular waits. I would tell a colleague the planning looks practical, but I would want to try the actual meeting practice before recommending the teaching.
